web.title: Booking Holdings CFO says even AI hyperscalers don't know their ROI — but he's learning from his 'AI coach' | Fortune
web.description: # Booking Holdings CFO says even AI hyperscalers don't know their ROI — but he's learning from his 'AI coach' | Fortune ... Booking Holdings CFO says even AI hyperscalers don't know their ROI — but he's learning from his 'AI coach' | Fortune ... October 2, 2026, 10:42 AM ET Ewout Steenbergen, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Booking Holdings at the Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange on October 1, 2026. Rebecca Greenfield/Fortune Booking Holdings’ chief financial officer thinks the companies spending the most on artificial intelligence are guessing. “I even think that the hyperscalers that spend hundreds of billions on the development of their large language models, they don’t really know what is going to be the ROI,” Ewout Steenbergen said Thursday at Fortune‘s AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange. “They have maybe some assumptions and some hypothesis, but the whole point is: you don’t want to fall behind.” ... Booking, which owns Booking.com, Agoda, Priceline and OpenTable, is telling investors that AI will make travel easier for customers and its marketing cheaper. The customer-side numbers are still small. Steenbergen said on the company’s Q2 call in August that referrals from large language models, paid and unpaid, were under 1% of total room nights. The clearer gains he detailed to Estrada are so far occurring inside the company. ... About one-third of Booking’s customers arrive through paid channels such as search, social media and metasearch sites, and the company spends $8 billion to $9 billion a year on them, he said. Booking runs constant A/B tests and large optimization models to decide where that money goes. The other two-thirds of customers come directly, and Booking is building AI tools into its own apps to keep them. Booking’s own AI tools show modest gains, he said. Customers who use them take a little less time to book, convert at slightly higher rates and cancel slightly less often. “It’s very early stage, so it’s not a lot of data,” he said. ... Steenbergen said the bigger opportunity is growth, not cost. Answering an audience question about trip bundles, he said Booking is “more transactional” today and AI could make it “a much more high frequency business.” ... Booking points to early signs in its Q2 numbers. Connected Trip transactions, where travelers book more than one travel vertical for the same trip, grew at a low-double-digit rate at Booking.com. Merchant bookings reached about 73% of gross bookings. Level 2 and Level 3 Genius members made up more than 30% of active customers. Steenbergen is learning, too. He said he has an “AI coach,” and he talks about it inside the company on purpose. He also has two agents working for him. One, which he calls a “strategic thought partner,” helps with board presentations and strategic plans. The other, a “critical equity research agent,” helps him prepare for earnings calls. “No one knows this,” he said. “If I have to learn and I have a coach, it’s very normal. Everyone has to learn.”

web.description: Lola, Booking Holdings' new AI assistant, books hotels, tables and tickets in one chat and charges members up to $25 a month for rates up to 15% below the public price Sep 30, 2026 by Markus Busch On Tuesday, Booking Holdings opened Lola, an AI assistant that finds and books hotels, restaurant tables and event tickets inside one chat. Lola charges the traveler for it. Paying members get hotel rates below the public price. The hotel still pays commission on those rooms. So a single stay booked through Lola can earn Booking Holdings twice: a commission from the hotel, and a membership fee from the guest. ... Kayak's co-founders, Steve Hafner and Paul English, built Lola in five months with about 20 people in New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. It is wholly owned by Booking Holdings, and Hafner reports to CEO Glenn Fogel. ... Membership comes in three tiers. Free. Plus at $5 a month. VIP at $25 a month. Both paid plans lock the member in for 12 months, which makes VIP a $300 decision. Hafner gave Skift the logic in one line: "If you pay us, we don't need to make money on transactions." The fee replaces the margin, and Lola says it passes that margin back as hotel rates. According to the launch release, Plus members typically save 10% at qualifying hotels and VIPs save up to 15% at four- and five-star hotels. Those rates come through Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda and Nuitée. ... When Lola sells a member rate on a room that comes through Booking.com, that room still carries a commission. The member's discount comes out of it. Hafner told Skift as much: once the member pays a fee, Lola no longer needs to keep the commission, so it goes back to her. The numbers line up. The VIP ceiling is 15%, and 15% is the base commission many hotels have paid Booking.com for years. The hotel pays what it always paid. Booking Holdings hands it to the guest as a lower price and collects a membership fee from her instead. ... Every hotelier knows the rate behind a login. Genius works that way, and the hotel opts in and pays for the discount itself. Lola's member rate is set by Lola, paid for out of the hotel's commission, and sold to a guest who paid to see it. ... Lola sells no placement. The release rules out vendor payments, featured spots, advertising and sponsorship, and the homepage repeats the promise. Hafner told PhocusWire he "used to love ads" at Kayak and runs Lola differently. It won't buy Google search ads either. ... Lola launched to a narrow audience. Its FAQ says members are admitted in waves by invitation, with general availability later this fall. The same FAQ lists Plus and VIP as coming this fall, so the hotel discount may not be bookable yet. Lola also describes Plus two ways: typically 10% at qualifying hotels in the release, up to 10% at four- and five-star hotels on its pricing card. Hafner told Skift he expects about 90% of active users to stay on the free tier. The model holds only if member fees outweigh the commission Lola hands back. Nobody knows yet which travelers will pay. ... When the paid plans open, ask Lola for a hotel like yours, on dates you know well. Put the VIP price next to your direct rate and your Booking.com rate. Then ask your Booking.com account manager whether the Lola rate is built on your Genius discount or your Payments by Booking.com agreement. Hafner says he wants Lola to become as big a brand as Booking.com. That would be a brand the guest pays for, selling a room the hotel already pays to sell.

The move places one of the world's largest online travel agencies squarely inside a fast-moving industry trend: turning conversational AI from a search helper into an autonomous agent that transacts. ... As reported by Android Headlines, Booking.com announced a new AI agent named Lola that can plan and book an entire trip. The report frames the launch as part of a broader wave of brands rolling out their own AI agents, positioning Lola as an end-to-end tool rather than a simple chatbot. Specific details on availability, supported markets, pricing integration and the exact scope of what Lola can autonomously book were not fully spelled out in the initial coverage. What is clear is the direction of travel: Booking.com is signalling that conversational, agent-driven planning and purchasing is central to its product roadmap. Beyond that, much remains to be confirmed, and hoteliers should treat capabilities as evolving rather than fixed. ... Lola's launch is best read as an opening move rather than a finished product. Several developments will determine how significant it becomes. ... The key takeaway for hoteliers is not to overreact to a single launch, but to recognise the trajectory. Agentic booking is moving from concept to product across the sector, and the properties that prepare their data, pricing and service accordingly will be better positioned regardless of which agent ultimately wins traveller attention. For now, Lola is a prominent marker of where distribution is heading — and a prompt to ask how ready each business is for a world where the first impression may be made not on a human, but on an algorithm acting on a guest's behalf.

web.title: [BKNG] Booking Holdings: Q3 2026 Earnings and the Long-Haul Drag on Room Nights | drillr
web.description: Published Sep 30, 2026 31 min read ... Booking Holdings runs the world's largest online travel platform through five consumer brands, Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK and OpenTable, and earns most of its revenue from accommodation commissions and the transaction revenue it keeps after collecting payment from travelers[1]. Booking Holdings Q3 2026 earnings are due on 2026-10-27, when the company holds its call on the third quarter of 2026, ending September 30, 2026[2]. In the latest reported period, the second quarter of 2026, room nights rose 5.3% to 325 million[3], gross bookings rose 9.0% to $50.96 billion[4], revenue rose 8.1% to $7.35 billion[5], adjusted EBITDA reached $2.648 billion at a 36.0% margin[6], and adjusted EPS rose 15% to $2.54[7]. On August 4, management guided third-quarter room nights up 3% to 5% and gross bookings, revenue and adjusted EBITDA each up 4% to 6%, with constant-currency revenue up 5% to 7% and currency trimming about 1 percentage point[8]. As of September 29, the analyst consensus compiled by Drillr stood at third-quarter revenue of $9.544 billion (19 analysts, range $9.444 billion to $9.733 billion), EBITDA of $4.762 billion, and post-split EPS of $4.48 (18 analysts, range $4.29 to $4.62)[9]. Three things matter most in this report. First, whether room nights stay inside the 3% to 5% range: second-quarter growth leaned on domestic travel while international room nights grew only slightly[10], and the guidance assumes higher airfares, reduced long-haul capacity and soft long-haul demand persist through the whole third quarter[8], so the results will show whether the Middle East conflict's drag on lodging is narrowing or spreading. Second, whether revenue keeps pace with gross bookings: merchant bookings reached 73% of second-quarter gross bookings[11], yet revenue as a share of gross bookings slipped to 14.4% from 14.5% a year earlier[5], and with identical growth ranges guided for revenue and gross bookings, the third quarter is the first test of the company's booking-versus-travel timing explanation. Third, whether marketing costs are rising: marketing expense was 4.7% of gross bookings in the second quarter, up from 4.6%[12], and the company said in its quarterly filing that free search traffic will keep declining in the short to medium term and could push up paid marketing spend[13], so the third-quarter marketing ratio and adjusted EBITDA are the most direct test of whether AI search pressure has reached the financials. ... Competition comes from several directions, and generative AI has made the contest for traffic entry points less predictable. The annual report lists competitors including other online travel companies, airlines, hotels and rental car firms selling direct, and companies such as Airbnb and Expedia-owned Vrbo that compete directly in lodging; it specifically notes that Google links travel search to Maps and its Gemini generative AI, and that other large technology platforms and AI-native companies are building assistants and agents that can search, compare and book directly, which could reduce visits to dedicated travel platforms[28]. Booking also depends on traffic from third-party platforms such as Google, and competition for placement in AI-generated results could raise costs per click and hurt marketing efficiency[29]. Because the company does not disclose brand or regional revenue or a quarterly direct-channel share, the competitive comparison here rests on the company's own qualitative statements and room-night mix and cannot be carried into a line-by-line financial comparison with rivals. ... This is the most important question because lodging generates about 89% of revenue and the third quarter is the year's highest-revenue and highest-profit quarter[16]. Second-quarter room nights rose 5.3% to 325 million and revenue rose 8.1%, both above the top of guidance[10]; but the growth came from domestic travel, and airline ticket growth slowed from 16.0% in the first half to 3.7% in the second quarter[3]. The company guided third-quarter room nights up 3% to 5% and revenue up 4% to 6%, assuming long-haul capacity and fare pressure last through the end of the quarter[8]; it also cut full-year gross bookings guidance because of slower flight growth while leaving its lodging outlook largely unchanged[32]. ... Marketing is Booking's largest cost, at $8.186 billion in 2025 or about 30% of revenue[20], and most of it goes to Google and other search and performance channels[13]. The company's annual report also lists AI assistants and agents that bypass online travel platforms and reduce direct traffic as a competitive risk[28], which is exactly the market's recent concern. The third-quarter marketing ratio and adjusted EBITDA are the most direct measures of whether that concern has reached the financials; the second-quarter baseline is marketing at 4.7% of gross bookings (4.6% a year earlier) and adjusted EBITDA of $2.648 billion, up 9%, at a 36.0% margin[12]. The evidence that the impact is limited is that AI channels are still tiny and the company's own channels are getting stronger. Management said traffic from large language models accounts for significantly less than 1% of room nights, with no material change in recent quarters[33]; the direct channel's share of room nights held at a mid-fifties percentage over the trailing twelve months[13], and the app share rose from a mid-fifties to a high-fifties percentage[11]; Genius level 2 and 3 members account for half of room nights, and AI voice support now handles most eligible inbound calls, cutting customer-service cost per booking by a double-digit rate year over year[36]. The contrary evidence is that the company said in its quarterly filing that free search traffic will keep declining in the short to medium term and could raise paid marketing spend[13], the second-quarter marketing ratio rose 0.1 percentage point year over year[12], and KAYAK has already taken a $457 million impairment because of expected increases in customer acquisition costs[22]. An alternative reading is that margin expansion came mainly from one-time savings in the transformation program and customer service, and once those savings slow, rising channel costs will show up directly in margins. ... , where KAYAK sits, and that line was $322 million in the second quarter, up 8.1%[5]. The transformation program lowers fixed costs and supports the adjusted EBITDA margin[27]. On second-quarter bookings, each 0.1 percentage point rise in the marketing ratio adds about $50 million of quarterly expense, roughly 2% of ... After the second-quarter results, CNBC's Isabella Gao argued in a September 9 analysis that treating Booking as a loser from the AI platform shift does not fit the operating data: LLM traffic is still below 1% of room nights, and while AI agents can plan a trip, executing bookings at global scale requires payments, compliance, live inventory and customer service, so Google's and OpenAI's early agent products hand checkout back to the online travel agency, with Booking a launch partner in both[37]. The piece also concedes that AI is genuinely eroding thin, top-of-funnel metasearch businesses such as KAYAK, argues that AI has so far lowered Booking's customer-service costs, and notes that a sizable part of the first-half slowdown in growth reflected dollar-based currency effects. This view points the same way as the company's own statements on the marketing-efficiency debate and offers a currency-based reading of the lodging-demand debate, but it depends on the premise that AI agents are just a new referral channel that will not materially raise acquisition costs. Between the second-quarter report and the end of September, this was the only data-backed outside analysis available, with other coverage mostly recapping share-price moves and news, and no equally argued bearish analysis appeared, so it should not be read as a shared market judgment.

web.description: # Expedia Bets Against the All-Powerful AI Travel Agent ... September 23rd, 2026 at 4:17 PM EDT ... Photo Credit: Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin, speaking at Skift Global Forum 2026 via remote video. Skift ... Expedia wants a seat inside the new wave of AI agents, including Meta's Muse. But CEO Ariane Gorin is betting on a messier future for travel: multiple entry points and specialized agents, not one bot that owns the whole trip. Speaking at the Skift Global Forum on Wednesday, Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin said she wants to work with  the newest generation of AI agents — including Meta's Muse — but doesn't think any single one can take over the entire travel journey. The company had just revealed on Tuesday that it would be available on Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Its X.com post didn’t detail how that would work, only that it’s “joining @Muse: tell it where you're headed and it can work with Expedia to sort your hotels, and everything in between.” Gorin, participating via remote video, didn’t elaborate. But she was clear about what she doesn't expect from this type of technology. "I certainly personally don't believe that a large portion of bookings are going to be an end-to-end conversational experience," she said. For her, travel planning involves several people, multiple rounds of consideration and, for some, what can be “a joy” of figuring out a trip.� ... - Expedia is joining Meta's Muse agent and will judge future AI agent partnerships case by case, on top of existing ties to Google AI Mode, ChatGPT, Claude, and Alexa. - Gorin doubts most bookings will become end-to-end chat transactions, and Expedia scrapped its single all-purpose agent for narrower point agents that each handle one part of planning. - AI tools have not lifted bookings yet, but they deliver more than 60% more data on traveler intent, higher engagement, and lower cancellations among those who book after using them. ... Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin used the Skift Global Forum stage to make a case for being everywhere AI agents live while doubting that any one agent will own the trip. Expedia confirmed this week that it is joining Muse, Meta's new AI agent, adding to integrations with Google's AI Mode, ChatGPT, Claude, and Amazon's Alexa. Gorin said she doesn't expect a large share of bookings to happen as one end-to-end conversational experience, since most trips involve several people and multiple rounds of consideration. Expedia abandoned its own single end-to-end agent in favor of specialized "point agents" that handle individual parts of shopping and planning, an approach its AI chief calls multi-agent architecture. The AI tools are not yet driving more bookings, but Gorin said they produce more engagement, more than 60% more information about what travelers want, and lower cancellation rates among people who book after using them. Asked why an AI platform should route through Expedia rather than go straight to hotels and airlines, Gorin pointed to fulfillment, customer service, payments, connectivity, selection, and bundling — the same argument Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel made a day earlier. web.title: Booking Holdings-backed Lola unveils membership model for AI travel and experiences assistant | PhocusWire
web.description: Booking Holdings-backed Lola unveils membership model for AI travel and experiences assistant | PhocusWire # Booking Holdings ... backed Lola unveils ... travel and experiences assistant By Abby Crotty | September 29, 2026 Kayak co-founders Steve Hafner and Paul English have revealed new details about Lola, the Booking Holdings-backed artificial intelligence (AI) assistant they are building for travel, dining, events and other experiences. The service will offer a free tier along with Plus and VIP memberships priced at $5 and $25 per month, respectively, with benefits including preferred hotel rates, dining access and travel perks. Unlike Booking Holdings’ online travel brands such as Kayak, Booking.com, Priceline and Agoda, Lola will not accept advertising or paid placement, a distinction Hafner said is central to building trust in a personalized AI assistant. "Don't get me wrong, I used to love ads when I was at Kayak, but that's not the way we're running this program. We're designing a tool that our members want. You need to be able to trust the tool to not be influenced by third party payments, just purely by the member's preferences." Hafner told PhocusWire. "None of our partners can influence our search results, and that's really important to us because it's a membership model, which means we want to differentiate ourselves by giving you the very best personalized results that aren't influenced by commission payments or sponsorships, and our results don't have ads on it," Hafner said. The project first became public in May, and an initial Lola.com page went live. The new announcement details the membership plans, partners and booking capabilities. The brand name Lola dates back over a decade. English first founded the Boston-based startup in 2015, with aspirations of building a consumer-facing app that would act as a travel concierge. The app relaunched in 2017, pivoting to focus on business travel and partnering with American Express Global Business Travel the following year. In 2021, Lola shut down its services, citing "new things to come" for the company on its website. ... Lola's launch partners include travel players such as GetYourGuide, Nuitée and Aero, as well as Booking Holding brands such as Booking.com, Kayak, Priceline, Agoda, FareHarbor and OpenTable. ... Hafner noted that the membership component means you can't use Lola anonymously, unlike other travel and experience sites. And that's intentional. ... The paid tiers offer added perks and benefits via Lola's partner network, and both Lola Plus and VIP memberships have a 12-month commitment. Plus members access preferred hotel rates through Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda and Nuitée, saving 10%, while VIPs save up to 15% on four- and five-star hotels. Both tiers also receive travel-related discounts on GetYourGuide activities and their first Aero flight. ... When a user decides to book, they can stay on Lola or leave. If they stay within the chat, payment is handled via Lola's APIs. ... , it's in real time, these are live ... . Not only do we ... There are also several plans for Lola, including the ability to link a Google account and book flights. "Lots of other brands are doing that right now—I don't know that they're doing it well," Hafner said of flight booking capabilities. "Kayak did it, I thought, pretty well, but it's not bookable on Kayak. So, we want to solve flights too. It's just there's other stuff we want to get to first." An agentic component ... "At some point, we'll get to be agentic," Hafner said. "The agentic component for us right now is turning a recommendation into a reservation. Someday we'll move on to anticipating changes in prices or changes in availability or cancel, rebook, that kind of stuff, but right now, recommendations becoming reservations—if we get that right, we're in good shape."

web.title: Airbnb rolls out travel map and social connections to drive discovery | PhocusWire
web.description: By Abby Crotty | September 30, 2026 Airbnb is adding social features to its platform, enabling users to connect with family and friends to see where they've stayed and properties they recommend. The updates were announced in May as part of Airbnb's 2026 Summer Release and are now available for users in the U.S. Once connected, Airbnb users can give each other access to view past destinations, as well as experiences and services they booked, which are visible on an interactive map. This feature also allows travelers to read each other's reviews, message within the app and save destinations to a wishlist. ... "Some of the best recommendations come from people you trust. Now, we’re making it easy to see where people you know have traveled, what they loved and where they’re headed next," the short-term rental giant said in its fall product update. Phocuswright research echoes this, with recommendations from family and friends consistently ranked as the top, most trusted resource for U.S. travelers. Broader views of different areas are also available through neighborhood pages on the interactive map. Users tap the map for an overview compiled from host and guest feedback, including information about what the area is like, what there is to do, etc. ## AI updates for guests and hosts, new service Airbnb is also rolling out artificial intelligence (AI)-powered trip planning features as part of its fall launch, including a new search bar where travelers can use natural language when looking for homes, services and experiences. Travelers will see AI-powered listing descriptions and a comparison feature, and within search, users can type keywords, with Airbnb's AI automatically selecting other filters matching that search. The company used the example of searching for "baby," with the system then pulling other related filters such as cribs, playgrounds or books and toy. Also this fall, Airbnb is launching AI-powered updates for hosts. This includes dynamic pricing, 3D floor plans for guests and AI-generated performance summaries. Hosts will also have access to a multi-listing calendar, allowing them to update different components across all of their listings, or across a select few, at one time. Services are expanding as well. In the U.S., users can schedule laundry pickup and delivery through Airbnb's partnership with Rinse and rent baby gear through a partnership with BabyQuip. Airbnb said laundry services are available in select U.S. cities, while baby equipment rentals are available in over 60 U.S. cities. In Europe, Airbnb users will now have the option to have groceries delivered, with meal delivery also available in certain cities.

web.title: What new research reveals about how travelers use AI to plan trips
web.description: Propellic ran a study to see what U.S. travelers actually do with artificial intelligence (AI), following them as they planned their trips end-to-end across five stages: choosing a destination, researching hotels, building a multi-day itinerary, finding day tours and the handoff to booking. Participants selected and used their own tools, recorded their screens and talked aloud while they worked. The full report will publish on September 30. Take a look at this preview of three of the findings now, because each one moves the ground travel brands compete on. ... AI told 71% of participants to book directly with the operator instead of through an agency. Independently, 68% said they preferred booking direct anyway. The reasons travelers gave were consistent: no middleman, easier cancellations and refunds, plus open suspicion that agencies push their own partner relationships ahead of traveler needs. The minority who favored agencies cited group pricing and human expertise. When online travel agencies (OTAs) did appear in an answer, they appeared as the booking link rather than as a brand the traveler had chosen. Propellic's 2025 AI research found very similar results, with roughly 80% of observed booking flows in Google AI Mode going operator-direct against 13% to agencies. That suggests the behavior and the results aren’t specific to Google AI Mode. It showed up across the tools travelers chose for themselves. ... Seventy percent of travelers said they trusted AI recommendations more than traditional search results. Another 25% said they trusted them about the same, on the grounds that the information was equivalent and simply arrived faster. ... ChatGPT took 47% of all tool use. Gemini took 22% and Google AI Mode 20%. Google's two surfaces (Gemini and AI Mode) are close behind in total, just split between them, and Claude, CoPilot and Grok shared what was left. Across a full week of planning a real trip, most participants stayed inside one tool. They didn't open a second AI to check the first, the way they'd open a second tab in search. Every traveler we watched who used more than one had ChatGPT among them, either as the tool they started in or the one they came back to. ... Google AI Mode ... Five other findings are in the full report, with the evidence behind each one and what we'd do about it. There's also audience-specific direction for hotels, tour operators, destinations and agencies. This covers things like how travelers handled the payment step, what they thought of branding, and some of the biggest aspects of the LLM responses that drove the purchase decision. Propellic also analyzed how they responded to ads in LLM results, and how they worked through planning a multi-day itinerary. AI is reading your content before your traveler does. That's the shift. There's a filter sitting between what you publish and who ever sees it, and it doesn't weigh the same way that search weighed. You can see it in all three findings. It sends travelers past the intermediary and straight to the operator. It builds confidence out of the shape of an answer rather than the words inside it. And it does all of that inside a single tool, with nothing behind it checking the first answer. Brand still matters. But the thing deciding what a traveler sees first is a machine reading for structure, specificity and claims it can verify, and most travel content wasn't written for that reader. The useful part is how early this is. Most brands haven't adjusted yet, so the gap is still open.
